newsitem.title: UK: New EU energy tax to hit southern Europe, not north.
newsitem.headline: New EU energy tax to hit southern Europe, not north.

text.p: European Union plans to set new taxes and expand existing excise on energy fuels could mean increases of up to 11 percent in pump prices for some, sources close to the European Commission said.
The proposals, which were mooted last year, will mainly affect southern Europe.

Greece, Spain and Portugal would have to increase taxes on some fuels to meet the new minimum requirement, but major energy consumers like Germany, France, Italy and the U.K already have taxes in excess of the proposed levels, the sources said.
The proposal would increase EU-wide minimum excise duties on petrol, diesel, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and kerosene, and set new EU minimum taxes on electricity and natural gas.
Energy industry bodies have mounted a campaign against the proposals ever since talk of the new taxes leaked out in December 1996, claiming the tax would damage competitiveness.

"There will be a significant impact to Europe's global competitiveness," said David Williams, managing director of the International Federation of Industrial Energy Consumers (IFIEC). "There's no doubt energy is already more expensive in the EU than other trading blocs."
Intense lobbying by industry groups is thought to have been partially successful -- the energy tax thresholds have been revised lower since December.
A Commission official said on Monday a revised draft proposes a minimum levy on unleaded gasoline of 417 ecu per 1,000 litres ($483) from a current rate of 287 ($332).
Leaded gasoline would have to be taxed at a higher rate than unleaded, but the differential would be decided by individual member countries.
Greece, Spain and Luxembourg would have to increase taxes which in real terms, adjusted for inflation could lead to between five and 10 percent higher pump prices in order to meet the EU minimum.
All other EU states would not have to increase excise levels.

The new proposed level for diesel of 310 ecu per 1,000 litres ($359) from a current rate of 245 ecu ($284) would see pump prices in Greece, Spain, Luxembourg and Portugal rise from between seven and 11 percent.

The draft would set a minimum tax of 3.5 ecu a gigajoule ($4) for natural gas used as a motor fuel while electricity would be taxed at 1 ecu a megawatt hour ($1.20). Liquid Petroleum Gas (LPG) would be taxed at 141 ecu per 1,000 kilograms ($163).
The above rates are applicable to motor fuels in general. The Commission is looking for reduced rates for fuels used in agriculture and public transport as well as for heating fuels.
A meeting of the Commissioners to approve the plans is likely to take place in March. If they give their assent the plans will go before the Council of Ministers later in the year.
